turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Got the obs done before you came in. Blood pressure's one thirty two over seventy eight, pulse 76, and the finger prick sugar was 3.8.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta. Mr Hale, what brings you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh, nothing. Bit shaky of a morning, that's all. She made a fuss.
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Dad, your shirt was soaked. Sweating, and shaky, and you skip breakfast. And last Thursday you were confused, you didn't know what day it was.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I was not confused. Just dozy, from a bad night. She's exaggerating.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): The shakes. How long?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, a couple of weeks. It's nothing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Most mornings, yeah, if I skip breakfast. Settles once I get a cuppa in me.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So you skip it most days?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Can't be bothered first thing. Tea and I'm gone.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Diabetic, yes?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Type two, years. Ongoing, obviously.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Gliclazide. Sixty milligrams, the slow release, in the morning?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, diamacron, the sixty. Well, the slow one. I take that.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every single day?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformin as well. What strength?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh, the metforman. Five hundred, twice a day, I reckon.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It's not five hundred. The box says one thousand milligrams, morning and night.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't guess that dose till the script's in front of me. Any chest pain with the shakes?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cough?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight gone up or down?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Did you catch the cricket last night? Smith was scratching around for ages on that slow pitch.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah I had it on. And the traffic coming in was a shocker, roadworks all round the oval, took forever.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I only saw the last few overs. That catch at midwicket was a bit lucky. Meant to bucket down this arvo as well.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Pouring by the time we're home, I bet. Right, sorry.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blurred vision?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pins and needles in the feet? With the diabetes.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. Late in the day, if I've been on them all afternoon.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sounds like morning hypos. Gliclazide on an empty stomach. I'll book a blood test, HbA1c and a glucose, plus kidney function.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): If you reckon. I feel fine sitting here.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't skip breakfast. Have something before that gliclazide, even a bit of toast.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. We'll see.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight, once those bloods are through. Reception'll book the test today.
[SEG0044] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him a bit of toast. And I'll bring the metformin box in.

spec.situation: Older diabetic on gliclazide and metformin with morning sweating and shakiness; skips breakfast; daughter reports confusion once; doctor reviews doses and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Patient said 'Not really,' not a definite absence.
bad.text: Shortness of breath (status=absent, assertion=negative, reported_by=patient, temporality=current)

bad.reason: Capillary glucose was completed by nurse, but transcript doesn't say nurse requested it.

omissions.text: Gliclazide was specified as slow release / Diamicron MR 60 mg taken in the morning; formulation/brand detail is missing.

Metformin dose is recorded incompletely/wrongly: patient said 500 mg twice daily, but caregiver stated the box says 1000 mg morning and night, and the doctor explicitly said he would not guess the dose until the prescription is seen. The record should reflect that the actual current dose is unconfirmed rather than just omitting the dose.
Shortness of breath was not a clear negative: patient answered 'Not really,' so recording it as definitively absent overstates the denial.
Weight change was asked about and not clearly answered ('Sometimes, not really'); this uncertainty is not recorded.
Doctor advised reception would book the blood test today / the test was to be booked today, which is not captured in follow-up/plans apart from the investigation being planned.
Caregiver said she would bring the metformin box in, a plan relevant to resolving the medication-dose discrepancy.
